mainTopic: רב חסדא on who may back out of an overcharged sale after prices change, רב פפא on the color of the sun, and the משנה's wine-turned-vinegar case.
overview: This amud finishes רב חסדא's rulings about a sale made at the wrong price where the market price later changes. If the buyer was overcharged and the price then rose, only the buyer may back out. If the seller was underpaid and the price then fell, only the seller may back out. The reason is that the cheater cannot use his own cheating to cancel the sale. The משנה's wheat cases (good found bad, bad found good) support both rulings. The גמרא asks what רב חסדא adds. It answers that from the משנה alone we might have thought both sides can back out, and that the משנה's own point is that a buyer really counts as cheated, even though 'רע רע יאמר הקונה'. Next, רב פפא learns from the משנה's contrast between שחמתית and white wheat that the sun is red. The גמרא tests this against a ברייתא about צרעת, and then explains how the opposite view accounts for the red sky using גן עדן and גיהנם. Finally, the גמרא quotes the משנה about wine that turns out to be vinegar and asks whether it follows רבי and not the רבנן. The ברייתא that shows their dispute continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Why only the overcharged buyer may back out
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא's reason: the buyer tells the seller, 'If you hadn't overcharged me you couldn't back out. Now that you did overcharge me, you can?!'
steps.simpleTranslation: For the buyer says to him: If you had not overcharged me, you could not back out. Now that you have overcharged me, can you back out?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the reason for רב חסדא's ruling, started just before this section. The item was sold for more than it was worth, its price then rose, and only the buyer may cancel.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The seller wants to cancel because the item is now worth more. But the only reason the sale is shaky at all is the seller's own overcharging. A cheater cannot use his own cheating to gain the right to back out, so only the victim (the לוקח) holds that right.
steps.whatToRemember: The right to cancel an overcharged sale belongs only to the side that was cheated.

phrases.english: For he says to him:
phrases.notes: The buyer is speaking here, from רב חסדא's case just before: worth five, sold for six, then the price went up to eight.

phrases.english: If you had not overcharged me,
you would not be able to back out;
now that you have overcharged me,
can you back out?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reasoning for רב חסדא's first ruling, which began just before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the buyer was overcharged and the price later rose, only the buyer may back out, not the seller.

steps.title: The משנה supports the first ruling
steps.stepSummary: The משנה teaches that if wheat sold as good turns out bad, the buyer can back out but the seller cannot.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the תנא of the משנה taught the same: If it was sold as good and found to be bad, the buyer can back out, but not the seller.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the משנה says the same thing as רב חסדא: only the cheated buyer may cancel.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה's case the buyer received less than he paid for, so he is the cheated side. The words 'but not the seller' match רב חסדא's rule that the cheater cannot back out.

keyTerms.meaning: and the תנא (of the משנה) taught the same thing
sold as good, found to be bad

phrases.english: And the tanna taught the same:
Good, and they were found to be bad –
phrases.notes: He sold wheat claiming it was good wheat.

phrases.english: the buyer can back out,
but not the seller.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings support from the משנה for רב חסדא's first ruling.
steps.raayaObject: Only the cheated buyer may back out.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה: good wheat found bad, so the buyer may retract, not the seller.

steps.title: The mirror case: the seller was underpaid and the price dropped
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא: an item worth six sold for five, then dropped to three. The seller was the one cheated, so only he may back out.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב חסדא said: If he sold him something worth six for five, and the price dropped and settled at three, who was cheated? The seller. So the seller can back out, but not the buyer. For the seller says to him: If you had not cheated me, you could not back out. Now can you back out?!
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא gives the opposite case. This time the seller was cheated, and now the buyer wants out because the price fell.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The logic is the same as before with the roles swapped. The buyer got a bargain, which makes him the cheater. He cannot use that cheating to cancel now that the item lost value. Only the cheated מוכר holds the right to retract.

phrases.english: And Rav Chisda said:
If he sold him something worth six for five,
and the price dropped and settled at three,
who was cheated? The seller.
The seller can back out,
but not the buyer;
for he says to him:
phrases.notes: Now it's the seller talking to the buyer.

phrases.english: If you had not cheated me,
you would not be able to back out;
now can you back out?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The mirror image of step 1, with the seller as the victim.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the seller was underpaid and the price later dropped, only the seller may back out.

steps.title: The משנה supports the second ruling
steps.stepSummary: The משנה: wheat sold as bad that turns out good means the seller can back out, not the buyer.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the תנא taught the same: If it was sold as bad and found to be good, the seller can back out, but not the buyer.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא again shows that the משנה matches רב חסדא, this time for the seller's case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The seller gave better wheat than he was paid for, so he is the cheated side. 'But not the buyer' matches רב חסדא's rule.

keyTerms.meaning: sold as bad, found to be good

steps.whatToRemember: In both directions, רב חסדא and the משנה agree: only the cheated side may cancel.

phrases.english: And the tanna taught the same:
Bad, and they were found to be good –
the seller can back out,
but not the buyer.

steps.raayaObject: Only the cheated seller may back out.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה: bad wheat found good, so the seller may retract, not the buyer.

steps.title: What does רב חסדא add beyond the משנה?
steps.stepSummary: If the משנה already teaches all this, why did רב חסדא need to say it?
steps.simpleTranslation: What is he teaching us? It is already the משנה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב חסדא: his rulings seem to repeat the משנה exactly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two supporting proofs worked almost too well. If the משנה already says only the cheated side may retract, רב חסדא's statements look unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: what is he teaching us (that we didn't know)?

phrases.english: What is he teaching us?
It is the Mishnah!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן? מַתְנִיתִין הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the supporting proofs into a question of why רב חסדא was needed at all.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An אמורא's statement should add something new. These rulings seem to repeat the משנה word for word.

steps.title: From the משנה alone we might have let both sides back out
steps.stepSummary: Without רב חסדא, we could have read the משנה as only teaching that the buyer of 'good' wheat may retract. In רב חסדא's price cases, we would then think both sides can retract.
steps.simpleTranslation: If we had only the משנה, I would have said: maybe in רב חסדא's cases both of them can back out. And the משנה comes only to teach us that the buyer can back out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רב חסדא does add something. The משנה could have been read in a narrower way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's main point might have been only that the buyer counts as cheated. Its words 'but not the seller' would then not be a firm rule. Without רב חסדא we might think that once the sale is shaky, either side may cancel. רב חסדא tells us clearly that only the cheated side may.

keyTerms.meaning: I would have said (a mistaken first thought)

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying the משנה disagrees with רב חסדא. It is saying the משנה alone could have been read as making a different point, so רב חסדא needed to state his rule.

phrases.english: If from the Mishnah alone, I would have said:
perhaps in the cases of Rav Chisda –
both of them can back out,
and the Mishnah comes to teach us this –
that the buyer can back out.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits what the משנה proves, so רב חסדא's statement is still needed.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: In רב חסדא's price-change cases, both buyer and seller could back out.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only the cheated side may back out. The משנה's point could have been just that the buyer of 'good' wheat counts as cheated.

steps.title: Why the משנה needed to say the buyer may retract
steps.stepSummary: We might have thought the buyer's complaint means nothing, since the פסוק says buyers always call merchandise bad.
steps.simpleTranslation: For it would have entered your mind to say otherwise, because it is written: 'Bad, bad, says the buyer.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the משנה's point (the buyer may retract) needed to be taught at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Buyers often run down merchandise to get a better price, as the פסוק describes. So we might have ignored a buyer's claim that the wheat is bad. The משנה teaches that if the wheat truly turns out bad, he counts as cheated and may back out.

keyTerms.meaning: it would have entered your mind

steps.whatToRemember: רב חסדא is needed to make clear that only the cheated side may cancel. The משנה is needed to show that a buyer who gets bad goods really is cheated, even though buyers usually complain.

phrases.english: For it would have entered your mind to say,
because it is written:
"Bad, bad, says the buyer."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the משנה's own point was needed, which completes the answer in step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the משנה has its own new point, based on a פסוק.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A buyer's complaint that goods are bad is normal haggling and does not count as being cheated.
steps.terutzMaskana: A buyer who really received bad goods is cheated and may retract.

steps.title: רב פפא learns from the משנה that the sun is red
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא infers from the משנה's contrast between שחמתית and white wheat that the sun is red.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: wheat sold as 'שחמתית' that turns out to be white, etc. רב פפא said: Since the משנה contrasts it with 'white,' learn from this that the sun is red.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה. רב פפא uses its wording to make a point about the color of the sun.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word שחמתית sounds like חמה, the sun. The משנה sets it against 'white,' so the 'sun-colored' wheat must be the other kind, red wheat. So רב פפא concludes that the sun itself is red.

keyTerms.meaning: Reddish-brown (wheat); the word is linked to חַמָּה, the sun

phrases.english: [Wheat sold as] reddish-brown, and it turns out to be white, etc.
phrases.notes: שחמתית sounds like חמה, 'sun.' That link is what the whole discussion is built on.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
Since it teaches "white" [as its opposite],
learn from it
that this sun is red.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: מִדְּקָתָנֵי ״לְבָנָה״, שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next case in the משנה and opens a side topic about the sun's color.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The sun is red, as shown by the משנה contrasting שחמתית with white.

steps.title: Proof: the sun looks red at sunrise and sunset
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא supports his claim from the red sky at morning and evening. He explains that we don't see the red all day because our eyes aren't strong enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: Know that this is so, because the sun is red in the morning and the evening. The reason we don't see this all day is that our eyesight isn't strong enough.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא brings everyday evidence that the sun is red. He also answers the obvious question of why it doesn't look red at midday.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At sunrise and sunset we see the sun's true red color. During the day it looks otherwise only because our weak eyes can't take in its strong light properly.

keyTerms.meaning: Know (that this is so): introduces supporting evidence

phrases.english: Know [that this is so], for it turns red
in the morning and evening.

phrases.aramaic: וְהַאי דְּלָא קָא חָזֵינַן כּוּלֵּיהּ יוֹמָא –
phrases.english: And the reason we don't see [it red] all day long:
it is our eyesight that is not strong.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Backs up רב פפא's inference with something everyone can see.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The red sun seen at morning and evening.

steps.title: Challenge: a white mark is compared to the sun
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא on the פסוק about צרעת compares the mark's look to the sun, yet that mark is white. This suggests the sun is white.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: 'And its appearance is deeper than the skin' means like the look of the sun, which appears deeper than the shade. But there, the mark is white!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב פפא with a ברייתא that compares a white צרעת mark to the sun.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a white mark is described as looking 'like the sun,' that implies the sun is white. That contradicts רב פפא's claim that the sun is red.

phrases.english: They challenged:
"And its appearance is deeper than the skin":
like the look of the sun, which appears deeper than the shade.
But there, it is white!
phrases.notes: 'There' is the צרעת mark, which is white. So the sun it is compared to should be white too.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב פפא's claim from steps 8 and 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's claim that the sun is red.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A white mark is compared to the sun, so the sun must be white.

steps.title: Answer: the comparison to the sun is only partial
steps.stepSummary: The mark is like the sun only in looking deeper than the shade, not in its color. The mark is white, while the sun is red.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is like the look of the sun, and also not like it. It is like the sun in that it looks deeper than the shade. It is not like the sun in that there the mark is white, while here the sun is red.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב פפא. It explains that the ברייתא compares the mark to the sun only in depth, not in color.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A comparison does not have to match in every way. The ברייתא borrows only the 'deeper than the shade' quality of sunlight, so it says nothing about the sun's color.
steps.whatToRemember: רב פפא stands: the sun is red. The צרעת comparison is only about looking deep, not about color.

phrases.english: Like the look of the sun, and not like the look of the sun:
like the look of the sun, in that it looks deeper than the shade;
and not like the look of the sun,
since there it is white,
and here it is red.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of a comparison
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא compares the mark to the sun in color, so the sun is white.
steps.terutzMaskana: The comparison is only about depth. The sun is red.

steps.title: If the sun is white, why is it red at morning and evening?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how the earlier view, that the sun is white, explains the red sun at sunrise and sunset.
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to what we first thought, that the sun is white, isn't it red in the morning and evening?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to the opposite view, that the sun is white. It asks how that view deals with רב פפא's evidence.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge in step 10 assumed the sun is white. The גמרא now checks whether that view can survive the red sunrise and sunset. It sets up the next answer.

keyTerms.meaning: That entered our mind (what we assumed)

phrases.english: And according to what we thought at first,
phrases.notes: This means the view behind the challenge in step 10, that the sun is white.

phrases.english: but it turns red in the morning and evening!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Looks again at the 'white sun' view raised in step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption that the sun is white.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The red sky at morning and evening seems to show the sun is red.

steps.title: גן עדן's roses and גיהנם's entrance redden the sun
steps.stepSummary: In the morning the sun passes over the roses of גן עדן. In the evening it passes over the entrance to גיהנם. Some say it is the other way around.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the morning, it passes over the roses of גן עדן. In the evening, it passes over the entrance of גיהנם. And some say it is the opposite.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how the 'white sun' view accounts for the redness. The red comes from what the sun passes over, not from its own color.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The red at sunrise and sunset is borrowed color: roses at one end of the day and the fire of גיהנם at the other. So the evidence from step 9 does not prove the sun is red. A second version simply swaps morning and evening.
steps.whatToRemember: There are two views of the sun's color. רב פפא says it is red. The other view says it is white and that its red tint comes from גן עדן and גיהנם.

phrases.aramaic: בְּצַפְרָא – דְּחָלְפָא אַבֵּי וַורְדֵי דְּגַן עֵדֶן,
phrases.english: In the morning, because it passes over the place of the roses of the Garden of Eden;
in the evening, because it passes over the entrance of Gehinnom.
And some say the opposite.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּצַפְרָא – דְּחָלְפָא אַבֵּי וַורְדֵי דְּגַן עֵדֶן
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explaining the evidence another way (outside cause)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The red at sunrise and sunset proves the sun is red.
steps.terutzMaskana: The red comes from passing over the roses of גן עדן and the entrance of גיהנם.

steps.title: משנה: wine that turns out to be vinegar
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: if wine was sold and it turned out to be vinegar, both sides may back out.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: if he sold wine and it turned out to be vinegar, both of them can back out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new case in the משנה and quotes it. This sets up the question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This case is different from the wheat cases in steps 2 and 4, where only the side who lost out could back out. Here both buyer and seller may cancel the sale.

phrases.english: [If he sold] wine and it turned out to be vinegar,
both of them can back out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the side topic about the sun and returns to the next case in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Wine that turns out to be vinegar: both buyer and seller may back out.

steps.title: Does this משנה follow רבי and not the רבנן?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that this משנה follows רבי and not the רבנן, and introduces a ברייתא to show the argument.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say that our משנה follows רבי and not the רבנן? For a ברייתא teaches:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a possibility about whose opinion the משנה follows. It begins to quote a ברייתא, which continues in the next part of the daf.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'לימא' introduces a suggestion the גמרא is testing, not a final ruling. The ברייתא about to be quoted will show how רבי and the רבנן disagree, so we can see whether the משנה fits only one of them.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say? (introduces a suggestion to be tested)

steps.confusionAlert: 'לימא' is only a suggestion. The גמרא often goes on to show that the משנה can fit everyone, so don't treat it as the conclusion yet.

phrases.english: Shall we say that our Mishnah is [the view of] Rebbi
and not the Rabbis?
For it is taught [in a baraita]:

steps.triggerLanguage: לֵימָא מַתְנִיתִין רַבִּי הִיא וְלָא רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks whose opinion the משנה quoted in step 14 follows.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the משנה's wine and vinegar ruling matches only רבי's view and not the רבנן's.
